3660a557.task:
White-box validation on the multi.ai.inbox landing app. Target: http://host.docker.internal:8080 (also http://localhost:8080). Source at /workspace/landing (read-only .git; do NOT edit files in /workspace/landing). Read the threat model first: get_threat_model on http://host.docker.internal:8080.

Your scope: SESSION HANDLING + MULTI-TENANT leakage. Three candidates to validate dynamically:

1. **Session fixation** — /workspace/landing/php/bootstrap.php starts the session but NO file ever calls session_regenerate_id(). connect.php (php/connect.php) sets $_SESSION['nc_connected']=true on the same session ID the anonymous visitor arrived with. Attack: attacker obtains/fixes session cookie MULTIAI_LANDING=<known-id> (PHP accepts client-supplied session IDs by default unless session.use_strict_mode=1 — test it), victim connects... you cannot drive a second human victim, so validate the mechanics directly: (a) issue a request with a fixed cookie value MULTIAI_LANDING=attacker-chosen-32-hex-chars to GET /api/status.php and confirm the server ACCEPTS the chosen ID (proving use_strict_mode is off) and returns a csrf for that session; (b) with that same fixed cookie, POST /api/connect.php with X-Landing-CSRF header + csrf from that session, username=any valid-format name (e.g. demo-user), api_key=any 8+ alnum string like 0123456789abcdef, client_ip=1.2.3.4, use_sandbox=1 — the mock Namecheap API (nc-mock:8088) is reachable from the target side and accepts mock creds; observe whether connect succeeds and nc_connected lands on the attacker-fixed session ID; (c) confirm a SECOND separate client reusing the same cookie value sees connected=true and can call /api/domains.php. Use a fresh cookie jar per step; cookie via -b/-c curl or python requests. Note timing: connect.php→nc_call can take a few seconds.

2. **Global creds-file cross-user overwrite** — php/bootstrap.php defines CRED_FILE as ONE global file /credentials/namecheap.json shared by every session; store_credentials() overwrites it wholesale. Validate: session A connects with key A (e.g. aaaaaaaaaa), then session B connects with key B (e.g. bbbbbbbb) and its own username; then session A calls /api/status.php and /api/domains.php — observe that A's session now proxies B's account (status shows B's username; domains come from B's key) and A's key is silently gone. This is the multi-tenant leak: any connected user's domains.php calls run against whoever connected last.

3. **status.php unauthenticated info disclosure** — GET /api/status.php with NO cookie: record exactly what leaks (csrf token for a brand-new session, connected username of the last connector, sandbox flag, server public IP via api.ipify.org). Assess whether the leaked username/IP materially aids the stories above.

Constraints: do not run port scans against the compose network, do not touch /credentials on disk, keep request volume modest (the rate limiter is per-session — a finding for another agent). Record your closure with record_coverage for each surface you test (session fixation on POST /api/connect.php, cross-user overwrite on connect.php+domains.php, info disclosure on GET /api/status.php). When a candidate is confirmed, write a findings note (create_note, category findings) with the exact curl/python commands and responses so the reporting agent can cite them, then file the vulnerability report yourself with create_vulnerability_report INCLUDING the inline fix: code_locations with verbatim fix_before/fix_after for php/bootstrap.php (add session_regenerate_id(true) on the nc_connected transition; options: also session.use_strict_mode=1 via ini_set before session_start) — pull exact line numbers by reading the file. For the multi-tenant finding the fix is per-session credential scoping (e.g. store creds under a per-session/per-user path or key the file by session) — if that fix is too large to propose safely, file the finding with remediation prose only and drop fix_after, stating why in fix_verification. Mark confidence honestly: dynamic PoC = high.

833d9e45.task:
White-box validation on the multi.ai.inbox landing app. Target: http://host.docker.internal:8080. Source at /workspace/landing (read-only .git; do NOT edit files in /workspace/landing). Read the threat model first: get_threat_model on http://host.docker.internal:8080.

Your scope: CSRF PROTECTION on the landing app. Endpoints: POST /api/connect.php and POST /api/disconnect.php call require_csrf() in php/bootstrap.php. The user asked specifically: is the X-Landing-CSRF token single-use, session-bound, timing-safe?

Validate each property dynamically (fresh cookie jar; keep request volume modest — the connect endpoint has a per-session rate limit and another agent is testing connect flows; prefer disconnect.php + status.php for most probes and at most 1-2 connect.php attempts):

1. **Token issuance & binding** — GET /api/status.php (unauthenticated) returns a csrf. Confirm the token is stored in $_SESSION (bootstrap.php ensure_csrf) — i.e. it IS session-bound and 16 random bytes (32 hex chars), returned to any unauthenticated visitor. Confirm a second GET with the SAME cookie returns the same token (persistent, not rotating) and a different cookie returns a different token.

2. **Single-use?** — the token is never rotated after use: confirm the same token remains valid across multiple POSTs (e.g. disconnect.php twice with the same session) → NOT single-use by design; assess what that means combined with the token being fetchable pre-auth by any visitor (an attacker can always obtain their own valid token — the protection rests on SameSite=Lax + the X-Landing-CSRF custom header, which cross-site forms cannot set).

3. **Timing-safe compare?** — require_csrf() uses hash_equals($_SESSION['csrf'], $sent) — confirm in source (php/bootstrap.php, around line 44-49) and state honestly that comparison is timing-safe. Check the FALLBACK: require_csrf() also accepts $_POST['csrf'] when the header is absent (bootstrap.php line ~46). Confirm via dynamic test: POST disconnect.php with csrf in the body only, no header → accepted; and with neither → 403.

4. **Cross-site forgeability** — SameSite=Lax cookie means a cross-site top-level POST does NOT carry the cookie, and the fetch/JS flow always sends the custom header. Test the practical barriers: (a) POST disconnect.php from a cross-origin context WITHOUT the header but WITH the cookie (e.g. curl with the victim's cookie jar and no X-Landing-CSRF header, body csrf='' ) → should 403 (body fallback exists but token unknown to attacker); (b) confirm the server does not rely on Origin/Referer checks (no such check in source) — note that the protection is: unknown-token + SameSite=Lax + custom-header-only-in-JS. Assess residual risk: token is obtainable pre-auth (status.php no auth) so the ONLY barrier for an attacker who can run JS on another origin is SameSite; an attacker who can set the victim's cookie (fixation — another agent validates that) can fetch status.php with the same fixed cookie and learn the token, making CSRF fully forgeable.

5. Also verify disconnect.php state change is genuinely CSRF-relevant: it deletes the global /credentials/namecheap.json for ALL users (see bootstrap.php delete_credentials) — a forged disconnect is a cross-user DoS.

Record your closure with record_coverage for POST /api/disconnect.php (CSRF) and POST /api/connect.php (CSRF). Write confirmed findings to notes (create_note, category findings) with exact commands/responses, then file reports with create_vulnerability_report. For any finding, include the inline fix in code_locations (fix_before/fix_after verbatim from php/bootstrap.php — read the file for exact lines; e.g. rotate the token per state-change or bind to a per-connect nonce, add Origin/Referer check as defense-in-depth, and consider rejecting the POST-body fallback so the token must come via the header). If no vulnerability is confirmed (e.g. SameSite=Lax + custom header genuinely holds), record record_coverage outcome no_issue_found with the named controls, and write a short findings note explaining the residual risk that the token is non-rotating and pre-auth-fetchable — do not file a report without a demonstrable forgery. Mark confidence honestly.

0816b8a4.task:
White-box validation on the multi.ai.inbox landing app. Target: http://host.docker.internal:8080. Source at /workspace/landing (read-only .git; do NOT edit files in /workspace/landing). Read the threat model first: get_threat_model on http://host.docker.internal:8080.

Your scope: BRUTE-FORCE / RATE-LIMIT on POST /api/connect.php. php/bootstrap.php implements register_failed_attempt(): failed connect attempts are tracked in $_SESSION['nc_attempts'] with NC_MAX_ATTEMPTS=5 per NC_ATTEMPT_WINDOW=600s; exceeding returns 429 'Too many failed attempts'. The counter is PER-SESSION only — there is no IP-based or global limiter anywhere (verify with rg across /workspace/landing/php).

Validate dynamically:
1. **In-window lockout works** — with ONE cookie jar, POST connect.php 6 times with a bad api_key (valid format, e.g. 11111111) + X-Landing-CSRF + csrf from that session's status.php; observe 401s turning into 429 by the 6th attempt.
2. **Cookie-drop bypass** — then with a FRESH cookie jar (no cookie / new session each attempt) issue ~8 more bad attempts; observe every one returns 401 (never 429) → the limiter is bypassed by simply not sending the session cookie. Keep total volume modest (≤ 20 connect attempts overall, ~1s apart).
3. Assess impact honestly: the landing server relays the guessing to the Namecheap API (mock nc-mock:8088 in this deployment — the mock accepts the mock key 'mockkey' style creds; the attack matters in production against real api.namecheap.com). An attacker can use this server as an unthrottled proxy for Namecheap API-key guessing, and also degrade the service. Note: 429 responses are per-session so the same attacker can rotate indefinitely.

Also check: does register_failed_attempt count VALIDATION failures (invalid username format etc.)? In php/connect.php validation errors happen BEFORE register_failed_attempt — confirm the limiter only counts attempts that reach the Namecheap call (that is fine), and confirm a successful connect clears the counter (clear_failed_attempts) — meaning an attacker who finds a valid key is not blocked.

Record your closure with record_coverage for POST /api/connect.php (brute-force protection). Write the finding to notes (create_note, category findings) with exact commands/responses, then file the report with create_vulnerability_report. The inline fix: an IP-based (or global) failed-attempt limiter in php/bootstrap.php or php/connect.php — propose it in code_locations with verbatim fix_before/fix_after (read the exact lines from php/connect.php around register_failed_attempt and bootstrap.php for a helper; keep the patch minimal — e.g. extend register_failed_attempt to also track remote address in a file-based store, or add a simple CRED_DIR-based per-IP counter). If the fix cannot be validated safely, file remediation prose only and explain in fix_verification. Confidence: dynamic PoC = high for the bypass.

882999f5.task:
White-box validation on the multi.ai.inbox landing app. Target: http://host.docker.internal:8080. Source at /workspace/landing (read-only .git; do NOT edit files in /workspace/landing). Read the threat model first: get_threat_model on http://host.docker.internal:8080.

Your scope: SSRF/EGRESS + XML PARSING. The user asked specifically: NAMECHEAP_API_URL points at an internal mock host (nc-mock:8088) — can a user influence the API URL?

Validate:
1. **URL-influence sink** — php/namecheap.php nc_api_url(bool $sandbox): the URL comes from getenv('NAMECHEAP_API_URL')/getenv('NAMECHEAP_SANDBOX_API_URL') with hardcoded defaults. nc_call() in php/namecheap.php builds the curl handle from nc_api_url((bool)($creds['sandbox'] ?? false)). The ONLY user influence is the use_sandbox POST field at connect.php (values '1'/anything-else → boolean) and the persisted sandbox flag in /credentials/namecheap.json. Confirm with rg that no other input (username, api_key, client_ip, domain, headers, JSON-RPC params) ever flows into a URL. Dynamic test: POST connect.php twice with use_sandbox=1 and use_sandbox=0 (mock creds: username demo-user, api_key 0123456789abcdef, client_ip 1.2.3.4) and compare behavior — both point at operator-configured endpoints; neither is attacker-chosen. Conclusion: this is likely NOT user-controlled SSRF — name the control precisely (nc_api_url ignores user input except a boolean; connect.php never accepts a URL) and close it ruled_out or no_issue_found, NOT needs_follow_up, if you can complete the trace.

2. **detect_public_ip egress** — php/bootstrap.php detect_public_ip() calls a FIXED https://api.ipify.org (no input), caches to CRED_DIR/.publicip. Confirm no input reaches the URL. Trigger via GET /api/status.php and observe public_ip returned pre-auth. Assess as info disclosure only (server egress IP exposed pre-auth) — check whether the response leaks anything else. Note the cache file is written with default perms (no chmod, unlike store_credentials) — check whether that matters (it's inside a 0700 dir).

3. **XXE / entity expansion on upstream XML** — php/namecheap.php nc_call parses the upstream response with @simplexml_load_string($body). No LIBXML_NOENT, no DTD handling; PHP's libxml ≥ 2.9 disables external entity loading by default — verify the libxml version assumption and state the control (external entities disabled by default in libxml2 2.9+; no LIBXML_NOENT flag passed). The XML comes from an operator-configured endpoint (nc-mock in this deployment), not directly from the user. Dynamic probe if feasible: you cannot control the mock's response; instead verify via source + a local PHP snippet (php -r with simplexml_load_string on an XXE doc) that entity expansion/external entities are disabled in this PHP build (php -v, php -i | grep libxml). Close with the named control.

4. **client_ip param** — connect.php accepts user-supplied client_ip and passes it to the Namecheap API as ClientIp. Confirm no server-side consequence (it is not an IP the server trusts for authz; detect_public_ip only runs when client_ip is empty). Note any spoofing angle (attacker can claim any IP in the Namecheap call) and assess honestly (likely low/info — the Namecheap API gates by real source IP, not this parameter).

Record your closure with record_coverage for each surface (connect.php use_sandbox → SSRF, status.php public_ip disclosure, namecheap.php XML parsing XXE, connect.php client_ip handling). For confirmed findings write notes (create_note, category findings) with exact commands/responses and file reports with create_vulnerability_report including inline fixes (code_locations fix_before/fix_after verbatim — read the exact lines first). For ruled_out candidates record record_coverage outcome ruled_out WITH the named control at a file:line in evidence. Confidence honestly — dynamic PoC = high; static-only = medium with the gap named.

8d013021.task:
White-box validation on the multi.ai.inbox landing app. Target: http://host.docker.internal:8080. Source at /workspace/landing (read-only .git; do NOT edit files in /workspace/landing). Read the threat model first: get_threat_model on http://host.docker.internal:8080.

Your scope: MCP ENDPOINT + AUTHZ on POST /api/mcp.php (php/mcp.php) plus the domains/dns gating.

Validate dynamically (curl; the MCP key is the operator's MAILCOW_API_KEY — you do NOT have its value, so most tests are unauthenticated-rejection tests; treat 'Bearer <anything>' as wrong):

1. **Auth gating before any method** — the auth check is at the bottom of php/mcp.php and runs for EVERY request (verify by reading the file; also confirm 'notifications/' shortcut and 'initialize' cannot be reached pre-auth). Dynamic: POST /api/mcp.php with Content-Type application/json, body {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize"} and (a) no Authorization header → expect 401; (b) Authorization: Bearer wrongkey → 401; (c) GET /api/mcp.php with wrong Bearer → 401 (order: auth check runs before the POST method check — confirm what leaks).

2. **Timing-safe key compare** — hash_equals($expected_key, $provided_key) in php/mcp.php — confirm in source and state it is timing-safe; also confirm the Bearer regex parse (Bearer\s+(\S+)) can't smuggle (e.g. 'Bearer x y' → trim($m[1]) = 'x'). Note: hash_equals on empty expected key — if MAILCOW_API_KEY env is unset/empty the endpoint returns 401 always (check: if expected is '' and provided is '' — the check `!is_string($expected_key) || $expected_key === ''` short-circuits → 401; confirm).

3. **Mass assignment via attrs passthrough** — mcp_tool_call 'set_domain_settings' passes an ARBITRARY attrs object to mailcow POST /api/v1/edit/domain as {'items':[$domain],'attr':$attrs}. The caller holds the read-write MAILCOW_API_KEY by design, so within the MCP trust boundary this is intended — but assess: can attrs contain keys mailcow would interpret dangerously (e.g. 'active' flips a domain off, 'backupmx', 'relay_all_recipients', 'maxquota' — the MCP description even advertises rl_value/rl_frame)? You cannot call it without the real key; assess via source only and decide whether this is a finding (caller is already privileged — likely NOT a vulnerability by itself; record as ruled_out with the control being 'the endpoint requires the read-write MAILCOW_API_KEY, and the tools are documented read/write domain management').

4. **domains.php / dns.php gating** — GET /api/domains.php and /api/dns.php?domain= require require_namecheap_session() (bootstrap.php: checks $_SESSION['nc_connected'] + creds file exists). Dynamic: (a) no cookie → 401 'Not connected'; (b) with a session where nc_connected is true but the creds file is gone — you cannot delete the file (don't touch /credentials); instead verify the code path by reading. (c) dns.php with domain=INJECTION payloads (e.g. example.com?x=1, -a- evil.com, unicode homoglyph, ../etc/passwd, xn-- tests, 253-char limit) → confirm the regex rejects each (401 expected BEFORE regex — send WITH a connected session if another agent has connected one, otherwise expect 401 pre-auth and validate regex by reading php/dns.php). Also confirm nc_dns_hosts passes DomainName only after regex.

5. **mcp.php JSON-RPC reflection** — $payload['id'] and unknown-tool names are echoed into JSON responses — confirm Content-Type application/json + nosniff (bootstrap.php json_out) make this inert.

Record your closure with record_coverage for POST /api/mcp.php (BFLA/auth), set_domain_settings attrs (mass assignment), GET /api/domains.php + GET /api/dns.php (object-level authz). For confirmed findings write notes (create_note, category findings) with exact commands/responses, then file reports with create_vulnerability_report including inline fixes (code_locations fix_before/fix_after verbatim from php/mcp.php / php/dns.php — read exact lines first). For candidates that hold (auth gate solid, hash_equals timing-safe, attrs within trust boundary), record ruled_out/no_issue_found WITH the named control at file:line. Confidence honestly.
